q: You're driving along a winding country road. How should you choose your speed?
options: So you can keep up with the vehicle in front
At the maximum speed limit shown for that road
So you can stop within the clear distance ahead
Fast enough to stay well ahead of traffic behind
explain: You should drive at a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear. On country roads, slow down on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A roundabout just past the bend
The road narrowing on the bend
A double bend, first to the left
A junction on the bend ahead
explain: This sign warns of a junction on a bend ahead. Where there are junctions, be prepared for road users emerging, and adjust your speed as a precaution.

q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic. Why should you leave enough space between you and the vehicle in front?
options: So drivers can't pull in front of you
So you can build up speed between stops
So you don't need to use your brakes
So you can get round it if it breaks down
explain: In slow-moving traffic, leave enough space to be able to manoeuvre if the vehicle in front breaks down or an emergency vehicle needs to get past. Never get so close that you can't stop safely.

q: You're approaching a blind bend on a narrow country lane. What should you be prepared for?
options: Oncoming drivers always giving way to you
The road being blocked just beyond the bend
The bend being gentler than it first appears
A clear road, as hazards on bends are signed
explain: Be prepared for unexpected situations, such as the road being blocked beyond a blind bend, and adjust your speed as a precaution. Bends can be sharper than they appear.

q: You're driving through a busy shopping street. A child on the pavement ahead is looking the other way. What should you be ready for?
options: The child waving you on to pass
The child waiting until you've gone by
The child stepping out without seeing you
The child using the nearest crossing
explain: Try to anticipate what pedestrians might do. If pedestrians, particularly children, are looking the other way, they may step out into the road without seeing you.

q: You're parked at the side of the road and about to move off. You've checked all your mirrors. What should you do next?
options: Look round to check your blind spots
Sound your horn to warn other traffic
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Flash your headlights at oncoming traffic
explain: Before moving off, use all your mirrors, then look round to check the blind spots – the areas you can't see in the mirrors. Signal if necessary and take a final look round before you move off.

q: You're about to turn left into a side road. When should you check your mirrors?
options: Once you've started to turn
As you begin to brake for the turn
Only if you hear a horn behind you
In good time before you signal
explain: You should use your mirrors in good time before you signal or change direction or speed, and give a left-turn signal well before you turn.

q: You're about to change direction on a busy road. Which routine does the Highway Code tell you to use?
options: Signal – Mirrors – Manoeuvre
Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre
Manoeuvre – Mirrors – Signal
Signal – Manoeuvre – Mirrors
explain: Remember Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre. Check your mirrors first so you know what's behind and to each side of you before you signal or change direction.

q: You're waiting to turn right into a side road and a safe gap appears in the oncoming traffic. What should you do before you make the turn?
options: Switch on your hazard warning lights
Sound your horn to warn oncoming traffic
Check your mirrors and blind spot again
Wave to the next oncoming driver to wait
explain: Before turning right, check your mirrors and blind spot again to make sure you aren't being overtaken, then make the turn. Don't cut the corner.

q: You're about to overtake on a motorway. A car you saw in your door mirror a moment ago has disappeared from view. What should you do?
options: Glance sideways to check your blind spot
Assume it has left and move out at once
Speed up so it can't come alongside you
Signal and move straight out into the lane
explain: Before overtaking, take a quick sideways glance into the blind spot area to check the position of a vehicle that may have disappeared from your view in the mirror.

q: You've just hired a car you haven't driven before. Your licence and insurance are in order. What should you do before you set off?
options: Rely on the hire company's checks
Set the mirrors once you're moving
Test the brakes hard on the main road
Find out where all the controls are
explain: Before setting off, you should make sure you know where all the controls are and how to use them, and that your mirrors and seat are adjusted correctly.

q: You've just turned right at a junction and your indicator is still flashing. Why should you make sure it's cancelled?
options: It will flatten the car's battery
It's illegal to signal on a straight road
It will distract your passengers
It could mislead other road users
explain: Signals warn and inform other road users of what you intend to do. Cancel them after use and make sure they won't confuse others, who may think you're about to turn.

q: You're driving along a main road and see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: The road narrowing on the left
A lane closing on the right
A sharp bend to the left ahead
Traffic merging from the left ahead
explain: This sign warns that traffic will be merging from the left ahead. Where there are junctions, be prepared for road users joining and adjust your speed if necessary.

q: You're signalling to move out past a parked van, but a cyclist is coming up on your right. What should you do?
options: Wait for the cyclist to pass before moving out
Move out, as your signal gives you priority
Sound your horn, then move out
Speed up to get past the van first
explain: Signalling doesn't give you priority. Cyclists are harder to see than larger vehicles and are particularly vulnerable, so give way to them when you change direction – don't cut across them.

q: The driver of the car in front gives this arm signal. What does it mean?
options: I intend to move out to the right
I intend to move in to the left
Please overtake me when it's safe
I intend to slow down or stop
explain: This arm signal means the driver intends to slow down or stop. Watch out for signals given by other road users and only go on when you're satisfied it's safe.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

q: You're waiting to join a roundabout. A car on the roundabout to your right isn't signalling. What should you bear in mind?
options: It must be going straight ahead
It's certain to pass your road
It has to give way to you
It may not be signalling correctly
explain: Watch out for all other road users already on the roundabout, and be aware that they may not be signalling correctly or at all. Wait until you're sure what they're doing.

q: You're waiting at red traffic lights and the phone in your pocket beeps with a message. What should you do?
options: Read it, as the car isn't moving
Read it if the engine has switched itself off
Leave it, as the law still applies at lights
Read it, but put it down before the lights change
explain: It's illegal to hold and use a phone while driving. The law still applies when you're stopped at traffic lights or queuing in traffic – even in a car that turns its engine off when you stop.

q: You're caught holding and using your phone while driving. What penalty can you get?
options: 6 penalty points and a £200 fine
3 penalty points and a £100 fine
6 penalty points and a £100 fine
3 penalty points and a £200 fine
explain: You can get 6 penalty points and a £200 fine if you hold and use a phone, sat nav, tablet or any device that can send and receive data while driving.

q: You passed your driving test 18 months ago. You're caught holding and using your phone while driving. What will happen?
options: You'll get a verbal warning only
You'll get 3 points but keep your licence
You'll have to take extra lessons only
You'll lose your licence
explain: Holding and using a phone can bring 6 penalty points. If you passed your test in the last 2 years, you'll lose your licence and have to pass both the theory and practical tests again.

q: Your car has a hands-free phone system and a call comes in while you're driving. What's the safest thing to do?
options: Answer it, as hands-free calls are safe
Let it go to voicemail and listen later
Pick the phone up to see who's calling
Answer it, but keep the call short
explain: Using hands-free equipment is still likely to distract your attention from the road. It's far safer not to use any phone while driving – find a safe place to stop first, or use voicemail and listen later.

q: You're driving and need to enter a new destination into your sat nav. What should you do?
options: Find a safe place to stop first
Type it in while driving slowly
Do it while you're queuing in traffic
Hold the sat nav low on your lap
explain: Don't be distracted by maps or screen-based information such as navigation systems while driving. If necessary, find a safe place to stop. You MUST keep proper control of your vehicle at all times.

q: You like to listen to loud music while you drive. Why can this be dangerous?
options: It's illegal to play music while driving
It can make your car use more fuel
It may mask other sounds around you
It can affect your car's electrics
explain: Safe driving needs concentration. Loud music is a distraction because it may mask other sounds – you need to be able to look and listen for things like emergency vehicle sirens.

q: You're on a long journey and feel hungry. What should you do?
options: Eat while driving along a quiet road
Eat while you wait at traffic lights
Eat on a straight stretch of motorway
Stop in a safe place to eat
explain: Eating and drinking are distractions you should avoid while driving. Keeping both hands on the wheel where possible helps you stay in full control, so stop somewhere safe to eat.

q: You've recently passed your test. Your friends in the car are being loud and distracting. What should you do?
options: Tell them you need to concentrate
Turn up the music to drown them out
Drive faster to end the journey sooner
Turn round to talk to them at junctions
explain: You're responsible for your passengers' safety. Don't let them distract you or encourage you to take risks – tell them you need to concentrate to get everyone there safely.

q: Your car has driver assistance systems, such as motorway assist and lane departure warning. How should you use them?
options: Rely on them so you can rest your eyes
As an aid, while keeping full concentration
As a way to free up time to check your phone
Let them take responsibility for the car
explain: Driver assistance systems are there to help, but don't rely on them or reduce your concentration. You're still responsible for the vehicle and MUST have full control at all times.

q: You're about to drive home wearing a pair of heavy walking boots. What should you consider first?
options: Whether they'll keep your feet warm enough
Whether they'll leave mud on the floor mats
Whether you'll need them at the other end
Whether you can use the pedals properly
explain: Before setting off, you should make sure your clothing and footwear don't prevent you from using the controls in the correct manner.

q: You're planning a long journey. How often does the Highway Code recommend you take a break?
options: At least 5 minutes every four hours
At least 15 minutes every four hours
At least 30 minutes every hour
At least 15 minutes every two hours
explain: Plan your journey to take enough breaks. A minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving is recommended.

q: You're driving on a motorway and begin to feel sleepy. What should you do?
options: Stop at the next service area to rest
Stop on the hard shoulder for a rest
Open a window and keep on driving
Pull into an emergency area to sleep
explain: If you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place. Don't stop in an emergency area or on the hard shoulder – use a service area, or leave the motorway to find somewhere to rest.

q: You're planning a long drive. Between which times does the Highway Code say natural alertness is at a minimum?
options: 6 am and 9 am
Midnight and 6 am
2 pm and 4 pm
6 pm and midnight
explain: Avoid long journeys between midnight and 6 am, when natural alertness is at a minimum. This is also a time of high risk for new drivers.

q: You've had very little sleep and have a long drive planned for this morning. What should you do?
options: Set off as planned and drink coffee
Drive with the window open all the way
Put off the journey until you've rested
Set off, but drive faster to arrive sooner
explain: Driving when you're tired greatly increases your risk of a collision. Don't begin a journey if you're tired – get enough sleep before setting off on a long journey.

q: Your phone is in a cradle fixed to the dashboard. You want to call a friend while you're driving. What does the law say?
options: You may dial if one hand stays on the wheel
You may dial while stopped in a queue
You may dial if the call will be short
You mustn't pick it up to dial the number
explain: You MUST NOT pick up a phone while driving to dial a number and then put it in the cradle for the conversation. It's far safer not to use any phone while driving: find a safe place to stop first.

q: It's dark and the headlights of an approaching car are dazzling you. What should you do?
options: Flash your headlights back at them
Switch to main beam to see better
Look straight at the oncoming lights
Slow down, and stop if you need to
explain: If you're dazzled by oncoming headlights, slow down and, if necessary, stop. Don't flash your headlights or use main beam, as you MUST NOT use lights in a way that dazzles others.

q: You're about to drive home after dark. You normally wear tinted glasses during the day. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Wear them to cut down glare from headlights
Don't wear them if they restrict your vision
Wear them, but only on roads with street lights
Wear them only if it starts to rain heavily
explain: At night or in poor visibility, don't use tinted glasses, lenses or visors if they restrict your vision.

q: You see this sign on the approach to a busy junction. What should you be prepared for?
options: A lane for slow vehicles
A closed hard shoulder
Traffic lights out of order
Queuing traffic ahead
explain: This sign warns that traffic queues are likely ahead. Be prepared to slow down or stop, and adjust your speed as a precaution.

q: You're waiting behind another car to join a roundabout. You see a safe gap in the traffic from the right. What should you check before you move off?
options: That your hazard lights are on
That the car behind is well back
That the next exit is clear
That the car in front has moved off
explain: When reaching a roundabout, give priority to traffic approaching from your right, and look forward before moving off to make sure the traffic in front has moved off.

q: You're about to move out to overtake on a motorway. Why should you check your mirrors carefully first?
options: Lorries often change lanes without signalling
You must signal before you use your mirrors
The left-hand lane may be about to end
Traffic may be coming up behind very quickly
explain: Before overtaking on a motorway, remember that traffic may be coming up behind you very quickly. Check all your mirrors carefully, look out for motorcyclists and signal in plenty of time.

q: You need to reverse out of a parking space, but a van parked next to you blocks your view. What should you do?
options: Reverse out quickly before traffic comes
Sound your horn and reverse slowly
Rely on your door mirrors only
Get someone to guide you out
explain: Look carefully before you reverse: use all your mirrors and check all around. If you can't see clearly, get someone to guide you.

q: You're reversing into a parking space. Where should you mainly look while you're moving backwards?
options: In the interior mirror only
At the door mirror on the kerb side
Through the rear window
Forward through the windscreen
explain: Look carefully before you start reversing, then reverse slowly while checking all around and looking mainly through the rear window.

q: You need to turn your car round. Which of these should you avoid?
options: Reversing from a side road into a main road
Driving round a block of nearby side streets
Turning round in a quiet, empty side road
Waiting until you find a safe place to turn
explain: Wait until you find a safe place to turn round, such as a quiet side road, or drive round a block of side streets. Don't reverse from a side road into a main road.

q: You're reversing to the left around a corner. What should you be aware of?
options: The rear of your car will swing out
Your mirrors will show everything
Your brakes will be less effective
The front of your car will swing out
explain: Reverse slowly while checking all around, and be aware that the front of your vehicle will swing out as you turn.

q: You're following a slow van and want to overtake it. You check your mirrors before pulling out. What are you making sure of?
options: The driver behind has flashed you out
The car behind is close enough to follow
Nobody is starting to overtake you
Your indicator is already flashing
explain: Before overtaking, make sure the road is clear enough ahead, that road users aren't beginning to overtake you, and that there's a suitable gap in front of the road user you plan to overtake.

q: You're driving along a busy road. How often should you use your mirrors?
options: Only just before you start to turn or stop
Only when you hear a vehicle sound its horn
Frequently, so you know what's behind you
Only after you've finished an overtaking move
explain: Use your mirrors frequently so that you always know what's behind and to each side of you. Use them in good time before you signal or change direction or speed.

q: Which of these is an exception to the ban on using a hand-held phone while driving?
options: Answering an urgent call from work
Checking a map in slow-moving traffic
Texting while stopped at traffic lights
Calling 999 when it's unsafe to stop
explain: You MUST NOT use a hand-held phone while driving, even when stationary in traffic. There's an exception to call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it's unsafe or impractical to stop.

q: Your passenger starts a heated argument with you while you're driving. What should you do?
options: Argue back so it's settled quickly
Turn to face them while you talk
Drive faster to end the journey
Avoid arguing so you can concentrate
explain: Safe driving needs concentration. Avoid distractions such as arguing with your passengers or other road users, loud music, eating and drinking, or trying to read maps.

q: The police stop you because you didn't have a full view of the road ahead or proper control of your car. How many penalty points could you get?
explain: You can get 3 penalty points if you don't have a full view of the road and traffic ahead or proper control of the vehicle. The police can stop you if they think you're not in control because you're distracted.
